title: Composition is multiplication
explanation:
Apply one transformation, then another. The overall effect is again a linear transformation, called the **composition** [1], and it has its own matrix. To find it, follow $\hat\imath$ and $\hat\jmath$ through both steps; their final landing spots are the columns of the product.

Order is written right to left, like function notation: in $AB$ you first apply $B$ (on the right), then $A$ (on the left) [2]. And order matters. A shear then a stretch need not equal the stretch then the shear, so in general $AB\ne BA$.

To multiply by hand: column $j$ of $AB$ is $A$ applied to column $j$ of $B$. Rows of $A$ dotted with columns of $B$ give the same numbers.
keyIdeas: $AB$ means: do $B$ first, then $A$ (read right to left).
Column $j$ of $AB$ is $A$ times column $j$ of $B$.
Matrix multiplication is usually not commutative: $AB\ne BA$ in general.

workedExample.problem: Let $H=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ (a shear) and $D=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ (a vertical stretch). Find the matrix for 'shear, then stretch' and compare it with 'stretch, then shear'.
steps: 'Shear, then stretch' is $DH$ ($H$ acts first, so it sits on the right).
Reverse order: $HD$ has columns $H(1,0)=(1,0)$ and $H(0,3)=(6,3)$, so $HD=\begin{pmatrix}1&6\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$.
Test on $(0,1)$: $DH$ sends it to $(2,3)$, $HD$ to $(6,3)$. Different, so order matters.

pitfalls: Reading $AB$ left to right and applying $A$ first.
Assuming $AB=BA$; it holds only in special cases.
Multiplying entry by entry instead of rows by columns.

citations.quote: This new linear transformation is commonly called the "composition" of the two separate transformations we applied.
You first apply the transformation represented by the matrix on the right, then you apply the transformation represented by the matrix on the left.
